info.name: Cookiepot API — Files & Onboarding
info.description:
The foundation layer added on 2026-08-27: object storage, the AI service layer, and onboarding.

Covers only the NEW endpoints. Auth and user management live in the first collection (`api-doc-2026-27-11:42:00.json`).

## Getting started

```bash
mongod --dbpath ~/data/mongodb --logpath ~/data/mongolog/mongod.log --fork
cd backend && pnpm install && pnpm dev
```

Run **Setup → Register a fresh user** first. It captures the token AND leaves you with an un-onboarded account, which is exactly the state the onboarding endpoints are for.

---

## Uploads are deliberately three steps

```
1. POST /files/upload-url   →  a row exists (status: pending), you get a presigned PUT
2. PUT  <upload_url>        →  the bytes go STRAIGHT TO S3, never through this API
3. POST /files/{id}/confirm →  we HEAD the object and flip it to ready
```

**Why not just post the file here and hand it to the AI?** Because then the file is gone — the user could never open a gallery of what they photographed, nothing could be re-processed when a prompt improves, and there would be no evidence of what an AI read was based on. Uploading and processing are separate concerns, so they are separate calls.

Two consequences worth knowing:

- **Bytes never pass through this server.** It would pay for the bandwidth twice and fall over on a large file.
- **Only the object KEY is stored.** A presigned URL expires, so a stored one is a link guaranteed to be broken later. Keys become URLs at the moment of responding — every file in a response carries a freshly signed `url` and the key itself is never published.

Step 3 exists because the server never observes the PUT. Without asking the bucket directly, a row could claim a file that was never uploaded.

---

## The AI layer

Nothing calls OpenAI directly:

```
feature  →  aiService  →  openAiProvider  →  OpenAI SDK
                       ↘  mockAiProvider  →  canned JSON in src/features/mock/data
```

`AI_PROVIDER` picks: `mock` · `openai` · `auto` (real when `OPENAI_API_KEY` is set, canned otherwise — the default).

Every call site has a stable **prompt id** (`ingredients.extract_photo`, `recipe.generate`, …) and the mock data is keyed by it, so a demo is deterministic: the same input gives the same output, instantly, with no spend. Results carry `meta.provider`, so canned data is never mistaken for a real read.

*No endpoint in this collection calls AI yet — the extraction endpoints come with the capture feature. The layer is in place and stubbed.*

---

## Onboarding

The **server** owns whether someone still needs onboarding. `user.has_onboarded` appears on register, login and `/users/me`, and the web app routes on that — never on anything it stores locally, or a cleared browser would replay onboarding forever.

Saves are per-step and partial: `PATCH /onboarding` sets only the fields you send, so a step that collects cuisines cannot blank the kitchen list a later step fills.

item.description: Run one of these first. Register leaves you un-onboarded, which is the interesting state.

exec: // A unique email per run, so this is re-runnable without 409s.
pm.test('a new account has NOT onboarded', function () {
pm.test('defaults are Nigerian + West African', function () {

request.description:
Creates an account with a unique email each run, so it is re-runnable.

The response now carries `has_onboarded: false` and the default prefs — everything the web app needs to route straight to onboarding without a second call.

response.name: 201 — note has_onboarded and prefs

request.description: Login also carries `has_onboarded`, so a returning user is routed correctly on the first response.

item.name: Onboarding
item.description:
Read what has been answered, save a step at a time, then finish.

These are the only write routes a `pending` (unverified) account may use — a new account IS pending, and gating onboarding on `active` would deadlock every new user out of the product.

request.description:
Everything needed to render and **resume** onboarding — including `available_cuisines`, so the option list lives in one place rather than being duplicated in the client.

`completed` is the server's answer to "should I show onboarding".

**Status:** `active` or `pending`. **Rate limit:** 120/min.

**Partial by design.** Only the fields you send are written, so this step cannot blank the kitchen list the next step fills.

These answers are real signal — the suggestion engine treats cuisines as a hard filter, so someone who picks only Asian and Mediterranean must never be shown egusi.

`difficulty` is `easy | medium | anything`.

**200** the full updated state · **422** `validation_error` (unknown cuisine, or an empty body)

response.name: 422 Unknown cuisine

request.description:
The first answer to "what do you have", so the first suggestion has something to work with.

**Deliberately a plain list, not a pantry.** Counts, locations and freshness belong to the standing-kitchen feature; this is just the opening answer.

Note the body sends both `Rice` and `rice`: the server de-duplicates **case-insensitively but keeps the spelling the cook used**. It is not our place to re-case someone's word.

**200** the full updated state · **422** more than 100 items

response.name: 200 — note the case-insensitive dedupe

request.description:
Stamps the finish and stops sending the user to onboarding.

**Completing twice is refused (409), not silently re-stamped.** The timestamp is a real fact about when someone joined, and quietly moving it would lose that. A client should treat the conflict as "already done, carry on" rather than as an error to show.

(A genuine race between two concurrent completes returns 200 — the outcome the caller wanted did happen.)

**200** completed · **409** `onboarding_already_completed`

Registered before `/onboarding` so the literal path is not shadowed by the router.

response.name: 200 Completed

request.description: The same onboarding state appears on the user object, which is what the web app actually routes on: `has_onboarded` false sends them to onboarding, true sends them to the kitchen.

item.name: Files
item.description: Upload decoupled from processing. Walk these in order: request a URL, PUT the bytes, confirm, then list.

exec: pm.test('starts as pending with no url yet', function () {
pm.test('the storage key is NEVER published', function () {

request.description:
Creates the file row (`pending`) and returns a presigned PUT.

The row is written **before** the URL is handed out, so an upload that is started and abandoned still leaves a trace we can show and clean up.

`purpose` is one of `shelf_photo · receipt · voice_note · recipe_hero · avatar`. It scopes the key and makes the gallery filterable.

`size_bytes` is declared up front so it can be signed into the URL — the bucket then rejects an oversized body itself, rather than us discovering it afterwards. Max 15 MB.

Note the response carries `url: null`: there are no bytes yet, so a signature would 404.

**Status:** `active` or `pending` — onboarding happens before verification, and photographing a shelf is part of it.

**201** ticket · **422** `validation_error` · **503** `storage_unavailable` (S3 env not configured)

response.name: 503 Storage not configured

item.name: 2 · PUT the bytes straight to S3

request.description:
**This request does not hit our API at all** — it goes directly to the bucket, using the presigned URL from step 1.

To run it in Postman: select a real image under **Body → binary**, and make sure `Content-Type` matches exactly what you declared in step 1. The headers are signed into the URL, so a mismatch is rejected by the bucket, not by us.

No `Authorization` header — the signature in the URL *is* the authorisation. Sending a bearer token here can confuse some S3-compatible endpoints.

Expect **200** with an empty body.

exec: pm.test('now ready, with a signed url', function () {
pm.test('size came from the bucket, not the client', function () {

request.description:
Flips the row to `ready`.

The server never observed the PUT, so it **asks the bucket directly** (HEAD) rather than trusting the client's word. Without this, a row could claim a file that was never uploaded and every later read would 404. The `size` in the response is the bucket's number, not the client's.

**Idempotent** — confirming twice is a retry, not an error.

**200** ready, with a freshly signed `url` · **404** not yours / does not exist · **409** `file_not_uploaded` (nothing in the bucket yet)

response.name: 409 Nothing uploaded yet

query.description: Opaque, from meta.next_cursor. A malformed cursor falls back to page one rather than erroring.

request.description:
**This endpoint is the whole point of decoupling upload from processing.** Because the file is a first-class thing rather than an argument to an AI call, the user can come back and see everything they ever photographed.

Newest first, cursor-paginated. Scoped to the caller — one person can never list another's files.

Every `ready` file carries a **freshly signed** `url`. They are signed per response and never stored, so nothing here goes stale in the database.

**200** `{ data: File[], meta: { next_cursor, has_more } }`

response.name: 200 — pending and ready side by side

request.description:
Fetch one file, with a **newly signed** URL.

This is how a client refreshes an expired link: it asks again rather than caching the URL. Presigned URLs are short-lived by design, and a client that persists one will be holding a broken link within the hour.

Scoped by owner — guessing another person's file id returns 404, not their file.

**200** file · **404** `not_found`

Registered *after* `/files/:fileId/confirm` so the literal segment is not swallowed by the parameter.
